feedback: If a pupil clings to the size rule, point to the X-ray case on the axis: shorter than visible, yet transmitted through flesh — the size ordering does not predict the outcome.
If a pupil over-generalises 'radio always passes', note that metal blocks radio and thick rock attenuates it — penetration depends on material AND thickness, not the band alone.
activities.intendedInsight: A size-only argument is only a stepping stone; it cannot explain glass vs brick vs metal and is broken outright by X-rays passing through flesh, so the determinant is really material-and-frequency together (pointing, as a KS4 stretch, toward how a material responds to a given frequency).
learnerActions: Lay radio (long wavelength), visible (mid), and X-ray (short wavelength) on a wavelength axis against ONE stated material — flesh — and note, for that material, which pass and which are blocked: through flesh, radio passes, visible is blocked, and X-ray passes.
State the intuitive 'bigger waves slip through, smaller waves get blocked' rule and test it against these three cases for the one material.
Explain why the rule fails: X-rays have a very short wavelength yet pass through flesh (while mid-wavelength visible is blocked), so wavelength/size alone cannot be the determinant.

As a KS4-stretch direction of travel, reframe the real cause qualitatively: it points toward how the material's electrons respond to that particular frequency, rather than the wave's size — not a computed account at this age.
activities.title: Break the size-only story with the X-ray puzzle

feedback: If a pupil says colour is an innate property regardless of lighting, re-run the coloured-object-under-coloured-light case: a red object under blue light looks dark because there is no red light to reflect.

If a pupil thinks comms-band choices are arbitrary, ask which fate the band undergoes where it must travel — radio penetrates many walls and goes far; visible light is trapped by walls but guided efficiently (not perfectly) down a fibre, and long-distance fibres mostly use infrared.
For the oven mesh, confirm the pupil assigns a different fate to each wave at the same object (light transmitted, microwaves reflected).
activities.intendedInsight: Colour, sight, and communications are all instances of the same three-fates model: colour is the frequencies an object reflects/transmits rather than absorbs (black absorbs almost all visible light, white reflects almost all), and comms bands are chosen because of which fate they undergo in air, walls, or fibre.
learnerActions: Explain why a red jumper looks red in daylight using absorb/reflect/transmit — stating what happens to the other colours that land on it.

Explain the opposite extreme: a black surface looks black because it absorbs (almost) all the visible frequencies that land on it and reflects very little, while a white surface reflects nearly all of them.
Predict what a red object looks like under blue light and justify it (it would reflect red, but there is no red light present to reflect, so it appears dark/black).

Match each band to a technology with the REASON: radio for through-walls/long-range broadcast, the microwave atmospheric 'window' for satellite links, infrared for short-range line-of-sight (remotes) and fibre, visible light for fibre optics.
Explain the microwave-oven door mesh: it lets visible light out (you see your food) while reflecting the microwaves back in — the same object doing different things to different waves.

Explain why you feel warm in sunlight through a closed cool window: transmitted visible and near-infrared sunlight is absorbed by surfaces (and your skin) inside, warming them, while the glass transmits most of it and so stays relatively cool.
activities.title: Fold colour and communications back into the one model

feedback: If a pupil predicted 'the soft sock blocks it more because it is thicker', contrast the actual results: the thin foil blocked far more than the thick wool — thickness did not decide the fate; the material did.
If a pupil claims the signal only sneaked through a gap, note that wool fully surrounds the radio yet transmits radio; the behaviour is the material's, not a leak.
Reinforce: name which fate each material imposed on radio (foil → reflect, wool → transmit).
activities.intendedInsight: Blocking is not simply about thickness; thin metal foil reflects radio while thick wool transmits it, so the outcome depends on how the specific material interacts with that specific wave (density is not a reliable guide either, but this demo cannot show that on its own because foil is denser than wool).
learnerActions: Play a small FM radio or a phone streaming a clear station.
Before wrapping it fully in aluminium foil, predict with a reason whether the signal survives; then wrap and test.
Before wrapping it (fresh) in a thick wool sock, predict with a reason whether the signal survives; then wrap and test.

Compare the two results — a complete, gap-free foil wrap typically weakens the signal greatly or cuts it out, while wool barely affects it — and explain each: the metal foil mainly reflects radio (a Faraday-cage effect) so little gets through, while wool transmits most of it; if some signal survives the foil, check for gaps or a very strong station.

Articulate the rule the demo supports: thickness alone does not decide the fate (thin foil blocked more than thick wool), so the fate depends on material × wave; note that foil is also denser than wool, so this demo alone cannot rule out density — use the fixed-glass sweep (same material, different waves) to show density is not the whole story.
activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: foil versus wool around a radio

feedback: If a pupil insists the wall blocks all waves equally or that the signal must leak through a gap, give parallel cases: glass transmits light but a metal mesh reflects microwaves while passing light; brick passes radio but blocks light — behaviour = material × wave.

If a pupil treats absorb/reflect/transmit as mutually exclusive labels, show glass simultaneously transmitting most visible light, reflecting a faint image, and absorbing much of the UV; the incoming energy divides and the split depends on the wave.

A full answer explains material-and-frequency-together AND transfers to the mesh, coloured objects (selective reflection), and the foil/wool prediction; a partial answer accepts radio-not-light but still treats the fates as fixed material labels.
activities.intendedInsight: The same wall is opaque to light but transparent to radio; explaining this requires treating wave-material interaction as frequency-dependent rather than a single fixed 'blocks everything' behaviour.
learnerActions: Consider a brick house with the curtains drawn so no light enters and the room is dark, yet a phone still receives a radio signal through the walls.
Explain in writing how radio waves get through the wall when light cannot, stating what the wall does to each wave.

Name the fate of each wave at the wall: visible light absorbed/reflected (so the room is dark), radio largely transmitted through the brick (some is absorbed or reflected, so the signal is weaker indoors).

Generalise: whether a material absorbs, reflects, or transmits a wave depends on both the material and the wave's frequency — a material is not simply a 'blocker' or a 'letter-through' for everything.
Transfer the same reasoning to the oven mesh, a coloured object, and the foil-versus-wool prediction.
activities.title: Diagnostic explanation: dark brick room, working phone signal
